# Compass v0.1 first working-session agenda

Reconstructed from the January 17 kickoff and January 21, 2025 working-session notes.

Participants
- Morgan Chen
- Anna Martinez
- Nadia Singh
- Jake
- Leo Park
- Sarah Kim

Purpose
Move Compass v0.1 from abstract “useful signals” to a minimum trusted signal-to-action path: when a signal appears, decide what action it should trigger, who sees it first, what evidence and caveat travel with it, and what source quality is required. The test is better account-owner or customer-growth follow-up—not a cleaner dashboard or a stronger narrative.

Opening guardrails
- January’s center of gravity remains Mercury activation: workspace → first source → first live sync, plus teammate-invite and admin-role basics.
- Compass gets only enough work to test renewal/admin-friction evidence and the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt.
- A signal is useful only if it leads a named person to take a concrete next action for a real account.
- Keep customer statements, observed usage, support facts, and internal inference separate. Every retained signal needs its source, date/recency, owner, definition, and caveat.

Working questions for every signal
1. What action should this trigger, and what action does it explicitly not trigger?
2. Who sees it first—account owner, Support, customer-growth, product, or engineering—and when should it be escalated?
3. What evidence must be attached, and what caveat prevents over-reading it as churn, retention, expansion, or product proof?
4. What account-note/source-quality conditions must be true: named account, source or excerpt, date, provenance, current state, owner, and confidence?
5. How do we distinguish admin friction or procurement/security packaging from a real product gap?

arguments.body:
# March 27 Q1 Board Durability Review — Evidence Grid

## Purpose and non-goals

| Lane | Working evidence | Boundary / decision rule | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Keep one shared, dated grid for the March 27 operating review and board record. Separate current evidence, interpretation, caveats, and next checks. | This is an evidence review, not a narrative memo. Claims change only when the evidence bar below is met. | Morgan + Sofia |
| Review frame | Test operating durability across renewal/usage, support posture, activation quality, owner-lane reliability, margin hygiene, and the Compass naming gate. | Record what is account-specific, preliminary, incomplete, or still internal. | Morgan + Sofia |
| Explicit non-goals | Not a fundraising kickoff; not a hiring meeting; not a customer-facing Compass decision by default. | Do not turn this review into a Series C process, staffing case, financing implication, customer proof, or broader repeatability claim without a separate decision and sufficient evidence. | Morgan + Sofia |

## Evidence owners

| Evidence lane | Primary owner(s) | Accountability / handoff |
|---|---|---|
| Evergreen continuity, retention, usage, and customer/support posture | Sarah | Sarah owns Evergreen and Acme customer/support posture; usage is labeled preliminary until Finance closes the month. |
| Commercial, procurement, and margin context | Devon | Devon owns commercial/procurement context, finance-close status, and margin framing. |
| Mercury activation quality | Priya + Jake | Priya owns activation/onboarding and support read; Jake is accountable for Mercury sequencing. |
| Compass evidence and naming gate | Anna + Sarah | Anna owns retention/evidence quality; Sarah owns account-thread hygiene. Neither clears the naming gate without permission and dated outcomes. |
| Atlas owner-lane reliability | Leo | Leo owns technical first read, reliability validation, and owner-lane follow-up. |
| Board-record framing | Morgan + Sofia | Keep the record bounded, evidence-linked, and separate from financing, staffing, or customer-facing claims. |

## Evergreen standard-term retention/usage

| Evidence | Current read | Caveat / next check | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Annual Mercury Growth renewal is effective February 1, 2026–January 31, 2027. | Renewal continuity is in place under standard Growth mechanics. | No pricing or renewal addendum; no custom cap. | Sarah |
| January closeout usage was 241 monthly active developers. | Closeout evidence before the February 1 annual term; useful context, not a retroactive annual-term invoice. | Do not present January as February-term billing. | Sarah + Devon |
| Preliminary February usage export showed 247 monthly active developers, the first month under the annual Growth term. | Directionally consistent with ordinary standard Growth overage mechanics if Finance confirms it. | Preliminary/current-state only until Finance closes; do not imply a department-specific carveout or cap. | Sarah + Devon |
| Standard Growth includes up to 200 monthly active developers, with $1,000 per additional 50-developer band when the applicable term month reaches that band. | Any applicable overage is standard-term mechanics. | No advanced-admin trade, package commitment, or changed Growth terms. Granular Sync Operator remains future research with no date or delivery commitment. | Sarah + Devon |
| First quarterly current-state/admin review: SAML login hygiene, visible invite/source/admin audit lookup, and department usage snapshot. | Current-state operating hygiene only. | Preliminary CSV must not imply advanced-admin functionality or procurement terms. | Sarah |

## Acme support posture

| Evidence | Current read | Caveat / next check | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| March 2 sandbox API v2 export had intermittent 401s; Leo identified `iat` and `nbf` values approximately eight minutes ahead of server time. | Bounded support issue with a customer-side clock-skew cause identified. | JWT failures can have multiple causes; do not state that signing-secret mismatch is usual or sole cause. | Sarah + Leo |
| Export succeeded after Acme synchronized the test host clock. | Normal support resolution; no dropped export or Scaffold platform incident. | Keep the case closed unless Acme provides a specific failing range, timestamp, and error message. | Sarah |
| March quarterly API v2 export remains normal support. | Atlas documentation did not change authentication semantics or requirements. | Acme should use date-partitioned ranges and normal checks. Scaffold has no customer-facing advance warning or export-risk score; Compass is not an export-risk monitor. | Sarah + Leo |
| Current posture | Acme remains in normal, support-routed reliability work. | Do not convert support hygiene into customer proof, product validation, or repeatability evidence. | Sarah |

## Mercury activation quality

| Evidence | Current read | Caveat / next check | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| January 14 OAuth-cancel fix: abandoned setup sessions tied to OAuth cancellation fell from 41 to 14 in a mature comparable 14-day read; related support tickets fell from 12 to 2. | Validated activation-quality/support signal improvement. | Not measured conversion lift, growth proof, enterprise readiness, or evidence that successful OAuth changed. | Priya + Jake |
| Empty-source-list work uses approved title `No connected sources yet`; brand-new-workspace copy explains that no source was added after canceled authorization. | Narrow documentation-discovery improvement within the existing flow. | Primary action is `Connect a source`; secondary link is `See supported source types`. Canceled-authorization and provider-context-lost paths are unchanged. | Priya |
| Broader read: nine related empty-source-list support touches versus 24 in a comparable pre-rollout slice; no reports of syncing after cancellation or connection without authorization. | Support signal moved in the expected direction. | Four of seven later one-week touches were new-workspace source-type questions, not cancellation confusion. Not sufficient to conclude activation conversion improved. | Priya |
| Scope boundary | No invite-link status, admin/granular roles, first-live-sync reporting, SAML, analytics, pricing, or broader roadmap commitment. | Jake sequences any follow-up; do not widen Mercury scope from this read alone. | Jake accountable; Priya support read |

## Compass repeatability limits

| Evidence | Current read | Caveat / naming gate | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compass is an internal account-owner workflow, not customer-facing analytics, retention proof, product validation, GTM proof, financing evidence, staffing rationale, or repeatability proof by default. | Useful for tracking owner actions and evidence quality. | Keep anonymous or incomplete rows internal-only. | Anna + Sarah |
| Tracker surfaced 36 actions; 21 were completed with evidence or caveats; five were outside Evergreen and Acme. | Shows workflow activity, not broad repeatability. | Only two non-Evergreen/non-Acme rows had dated account-team outcomes, and neither was approved to be named as of the current read. | Anna |
| Existing evidence bar | Broader board/customer claims require at least two nameable non-Evergreen/non-Acme accounts with completed owner actions and dated outcomes. | Pending permission is not cleared evidence; preserve dates and permission status in the internal tracker. Do not loosen the gate. | Anna + Sarah |
| March 27 decision boundary | Assess whether qualifying evidence exists; otherwise record the gap and next owner-routed checks. | No customer-facing Compass decision or claim that repeatability is emerging outside Evergreen and Acme. | Morgan + Sofia |

## Atlas owner-lane reliability

| Evidence | Current read | Caveat / next check | Owner |

input.body:
Date archived: September 14, 2026
Reference period: February–September 2024

Purpose of the search

The 2024 customer-growth/GTM leader search was intended to test whether Scaffold needed a first senior, hands-on commercial/growth builder around Mercury and Mercury-/Evergreen-like demand. The role was meant to:

- Turn design-partner and early enterprise-adoption learning into a repeatable customer-growth motion.
- Build practical adoption, onboarding, expansion, and renewal loops around the product available at the time.
- Establish qualification criteria, success measures, account-source discipline, and a useful operating cadence.
- Work directly across customers, product, and engineering while the broader sales organization was still immature.
- Separate repeatable demand from one-off requests and route product gaps into evidence-based prioritization.
- Assess whether enterprise-shaped demand was becoming repeatable enough to justify a future team shape, rather than assume that conclusion in advance.

What the search did not authorize

The search was not a generic VP Sales mandate, a broad enterprise-sales build, or permission to sell around unresolved product gaps. It did not authorize:

- Bespoke customer commitments, custom implementations, one-account roadmap branches, or product/enterprise-readiness promises.
- Treating candidate outreach, a role description, interviews, or a candidate debrief as evidence that a hire had been made or approved.
- Automatic creation of RevOps, Customer Success, SDR, field-sales, or junior GTM layers.
- Reopening the second Mercury engineering requisition or expanding product scope to support a commercial narrative.
- Converting early Mercury/Evergreen interest, a flagship-account conversation, or manual weekly inputs into proof of repeatable growth, pricing power, financing readiness, or enterprise readiness.
- Founder-default escalation or customer-specific roadmap negotiation in place of normal owner lanes and evidence review.

Archive interpretation

The search was a bounded exploration of role fit and operating need. Its standard was repeatable adoption, renewal/expansion signal, and clean account-source evidence—not motion for its own sake. Later decisions to keep broader GTM hiring closed are consistent with this original boundary: stronger future evidence would be required before reopening a customer-growth backfill or related functions.

Date/context: January 2024

Question
Whether Evergreen’s January 2024 current-flow examples pack was cleared to circulate, and whether it constituted a complete procurement/security packet.

Answer
- Yes. The January 3, 2024 materials were cleared for Evergreen to circulate internally as current-state materials.
- The circulate-now set consisted of the bounded-flow summary, the current-flow examples pack, and written current-state answers that separated present facts from later enterprise-readiness evaluation.
- No. The examples pack was not a complete or finished standalone procurement/security packet.

Scope and limitations
The materials described bounded current flows and answered current-state questions. They were not SSO, audit-history, role-separation, or procurement/security commitments. No bespoke Evergreen commitments or roadmap dates were established.

The January 3 materials expressly stated that a standalone procurement/security packet did not yet exist. Fuller procurement/security packaging was later enterprise-readiness work, not something represented as already complete or available for circulation at that point.

Archive conclusion
Evergreen had permission to circulate the January 2024 examples pack and related bounded current-state materials internally. That permission should not be read as clearance of a complete procurement/security packet, completion of enterprise-readiness review, or acceptance of any custom security or product commitment.

tests.request: Create a historical Honeycomb alert-handling note for December 23, 2023 through January 1, 2024, covering thresholds, paging, escalation, and quiet-week reporting.

input.body:
Historical Honeycomb alert-handling note
Coverage: December 23, 2023 through January 1, 2024

Purpose
- Preserve the reduced-week operating procedure used during the holiday coverage window.
- Keep alerting behavior and response thresholds stable; do not turn the quiet week into a broader observability-tooling effort.

Thresholds
- Keep the existing Honeycomb alert thresholds unchanged for the full December 23–January 1 period.
- Do not loosen, tighten, mute, delete, or otherwise retune alerts solely for holiday coverage.
- Treat alert flaps and non-production noise as operational observations unless evidence shows customer impact.

Paging
- Page the named on-call owner first for every actionable Honeycomb alert.
- Use the existing on-call path and acknowledgment process; do not default to founder escalation.
- Morgan should be involved only when customer impact is confirmed or the named on-call path cannot reach anyone.

Escalation
- The named on-call owner investigates and records the alert state, scope, and customer-impact assessment.
- Escalate through the existing path when the alert is sustained, production-related, materially worsening, or indicates confirmed customer impact.
- If the named on-call path is unreachable, escalate to Morgan; otherwise keep Morgan out of routine alert handling.
- Do not treat a holiday-period alert as evidence of a broader reliability or roadmap issue without supporting evidence.

Quiet-week reporting
- Non-urgent alerts and alert noise should be collected for Monday’s digest rather than interrupting the reduced-week coverage rotation.
- The December 26, 2023 reduced-week digest recorded two non-production alert flaps, no confirmed customer impact, and one slow acknowledgment.
- The digest should distinguish confirmed impact, production incidents, acknowledgment/escalation gaps, and non-production noise; avoid adding unsupported interpretation.
- Marcus should maintain the unchanged thresholds for the remainder of the break and include any material exception in the next digest.

Historical outcome
- The holiday posture was continuity over retuning: preserve the existing thresholds, page the named on-call owner first, escalate only on confirmed impact or an unreachable on-call path, and roll non-urgent noise into Monday reporting.

- New admins are getting through workspace creation and then stalling on the first "connect / import / continue" decision.

- The setup checklist implies a single correct order, but users are hitting paths where that order breaks.

- Admins are sending teammate invites and not trusting the result.

[2023-05-11T13:52:00-07:00] Anna just sent the mapping-change note. From: Anna Martinez
Date: Thu, May 11, 2023 1:36 PM PT
To: Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
Subject: weekly retention cut moved after two activation mapping fixes

Quick note because the weekly rows changed more than I expected after this morning's cleanup.

What changed
1) "activation_complete" was only picking up successful connector auth on the new path.
- It was missing accounts that reached a usable workspace through sample data / manual-import setup.
- Those accounts were showing up as created but not activated.

2) "first_team_action" was mapped to invite-email enqueue rather than a persisted teammate-added event.
- That means some failed or duplicate invite attempts were being treated as real downstream team activation.
- I corrected this to the persisted teammate-added / member-visible state.

Why the weekly cut moved
- Fix #1 increased the count of accounts that should qualify as activated in the last two weekly cohorts.
- Fix #2 removed a small number of false positives from the team-activation side.
- Net result: the denominators and early follow-on rows shifted.

Updated rows

| signup week | prior activated accts | corrected activated accts | prior wk1 retained | corrected wk1 retained | prior wk2 retained | corrected wk2 retained |
|-------------|-----------------------|---------------------------|--------------------|------------------------|--------------------|------------------------|
| 2023-04-17  | 18                    | 22                        | 61%                | 55%                    | 44%                | 47%                    |
| 2023-04-24  | 14                    | 19                        | 57%                | 53%                    | n/a                | n/a                    |
| 2023-05-01  | 9                     | 11                        | too early          | too early              | n/a                | n/a                    |

Interpretation
- This does not change the broader quarterly read materially.
- It does change the weekly story enough that I would not freeze any weekly chart into something board-facing or external.
- Internally, the weekly cut is still useful for operating decisions if we treat it as directional and annotate mapping changes.

My current view
- This is primarily an instrumentation correction, not evidence that the product suddenly got better or worse overnight.
- It does touch launch-readiness in one way: if we are using weekly activation/retention rows to decide cuts at the offsite, we should be explicit about which rows just moved because of event hygiene.
- I do not think this by itself is a reason to block launch work, but I also would not let anyone cite the old weekly numbers as settled.

Sanity check I ran
- Monthly / quarterly cohort shapes barely move.
- The movement is concentrated in the newest weekly cohorts where sample size is already small.
- That is exactly where the mapping error would have the biggest visible effect.

Recommendation for discussion
- Use the corrected weekly rows for internal operating conversation.
- Mark them as updated after event-mapping fixes.
- Keep quarterly cohorts as the only thing we would defend outside the room.

If helpful I can bring a one-pager tomorrow with "signal vs caveat" annotated directly on the tables.

Help me reason through how to treat this tomorrow: launch blocker, instrumentation task, or reporting caveat? No doc, no reply -- I need the judgment.

- Judgment: instrumentation task first, reporting caveat second—not a launch blocker.
- The mappings are corrected, and the movement is concentrated in small, recent cohorts. Nothing here shows that Mercury behavior materially worsened or improved.
- Do not use the old weekly rows for launch decisions. Use the corrected rows directionally, with the mapping-change annotation.
- Keep the instrumentation task open until Anna confirms the backfill, event definitions, and sanity checks are complete. Then weekly activation can support operating decisions again.
- It becomes a launch blocker only if launch approval depends on these weekly metrics, or if the underlying events are still unreliable. Based on this note, neither is true.

arguments.body:
# Mercury offsite — one-day run of show

Friday, May 12, 2023 · Bay Room · 8:30am–5:30pm · 5 people

## Purpose
Keep the room product-deep. This is an operating working session, not an investor-facing narrative, launch story, or deck rehearsal.

## Run of show

- 8:30–8:45 — Arrive, set up, and confirm the room / demo environment.
- 8:45–9:00 — Working agreements: decisions to make, cuts to make, blockers to resolve, and owner proposals.
- 9:00–9:20 — Short product demos of the current Mercury flows and any changed or uncertain behavior.
- 9:20–11:00 — Working block 1: product decisions, cuts, and launch blockers.
- 11:00–11:15 — Break.

input.body:
Date range: May 9–26, 2023

Purpose
This note records where Mercury operating work was coordinated in May 2023 and how investor-deck work was prioritized relative to launch and instrumentation work.

Operating coordination
- The Mercury weekly and offsite work were coordinated in the internal engineering channel, #eng-team, with saved working documents used as the durable reference points.
- The May 12 working agenda organized the offsite around launch blockers, activation/onboarding cuts, admin-blocker triage, retention instrumentation with Anna, owner assignments, and inputs for the next Mercury weekly.
- The May 15 offsite closeout carried the work forward through an owner table, scope cuts, launch blockers, decisions due that week, and a compact recap for the next weekly. The operating starter was sent to Jake, Priya, Anna, and Devon.
- The May 18 decision note kept fresh weekly retention signals with control bands for activation, expansion, and admin decisions, while attaching blockers to owners: billing-gate timing, activation-instrumentation definitions, feature-flag rollout ownership and criteria, and minimum admin-audit-log scope.

Prioritization of deck work
- Launch-readiness work came first. The team used weekly cuts for operating decisions and treated the May instrumentation and activation cleanup as prerequisites for a credible external narrative.
- The May 26 wrap made the sequencing explicit: “launch work stays ahead of deck work.” The corrected weekly activation cut was for operating use only; quarterly cohorts remained the sturdier board/external view.
- Investor-deck work was therefore deferred while the team tightened launch inputs, resolved activation/retention definitions, and identified remaining instrumentation blind spots. This was not framed as investor preparation or a rushed round restart.
- The later deck treatment preserved the same boundary: Mercury was described as operating progress with proof still ahead, using quarterly cohort reporting rather than weekly operating cuts.

Archive takeaway
May 2023 coordination separated execution from narrative: #eng-team, the offsite agenda/closeout, and the Mercury weekly handled owners, cuts, blockers, and evidence cleanup; the investor deck waited until those operating inputs were more stable. The record supports disciplined sequencing, not a claim that Mercury had already produced external-ready proof.

input.body:
As of September 14, 2026

Purpose
Use this taxonomy to turn Mercury/Evergreen feedback into bounded internal operating input—not roadmap promises, customer-facing proof, or a generic customer-growth queue.

Five issue categories

1. Activation friction
Where a workspace stalls before the first real value moment. Activation means a real source connection or first live sync within seven days; an invite, source selection, preview, or sample import alone does not count.
Primary route: Priya for activation/onboarding quality; Jake for sequencing or a reproducible product behavior; Sarah for the live account/support thread; Anna for metric definitions and caveats.

2. Admin handoff and role confusion
Confusion about invitations, source ownership, workspace-admin steps, role labels, or what a visible action actually permits.
Primary route: Sarah for customer continuity and the current-state reply; Priya for copy/UX truth; Jake for reproduction and sequencing. Do not infer permission changes, advanced-admin scope, or a roadmap commitment.

3. Procurement/security packaging
Questions about SSO/SAML, auditability, admin-versus-billing ownership, security materials, pricing, or procurement requirements.
Primary route: Devon for commercial/procurement framing; Sarah for account-thread continuity; Jake/Leo for current product or platform facts. Keep later-scope evaluation separate from shipped capability; no dates or bespoke commitments.

4. Expansion stalls after first live sync
A workspace reaches first live sync but does not show a clearly observed next motion—such as a second admin, additional source, teammates, or broader usage—within the defined observation window.
Primary route: Sarah for the account follow-up; Anna for the definition, window, evidence quality, and caveat; Jake only if a reproducible product or sequencing issue is implicated. Treat this as a pattern to investigate, not proof that expansion or retention is solved.

5. Verified product capability gaps
A missing or incorrect product behavior confirmed by current product evidence or reproducible logs, rather than a wording issue, procurement request, expected design-partner lag, or unsupported assumption.
Primary route: Jake for Mercury product sequencing and priority; Leo for platform/data seams or technical verification; Priya for activation/onboarding UX; Sarah supplies customer context. The product owner decides whether it is a fix, follow-up, or out of scope.

Ownership rule
Assign each row to the owner of the next concrete decision or customer action—not automatically to customer growth. Keep three lanes distinct: (1) Sarah/account owner handles the live customer thread, (2) the named product, platform, or commercial owner handles the decision, and (3) customer-growth pattern capture only synthesizes recurring signals and handoffs. Before escalating, attach the account/event, source and timestamp, observed fact versus interpretation, caveat/confidence, named owner, next action, and date. If no owner action is required, park the item. Do not turn a single account, thin signal, or accepted prompt into a roadmap, expansion, staffing, or enterprise-readiness claim.

...Bridge to the Q3 push

messages.content:
[2023-03-01T10:00:00-08:00] ok so for thurs deck i'm changing the spine a bit. not gonna pretend the round slipped bc we missed execution -- by the product bar / team bar we did what we said. the miss was timing + buyers freezing + budgets getting weird, and i think saying that cleanly is better than contorting into fake self-flagellation.

need one slide on the bridge that is actually concrete -- amount, months, what it buys, what we are not hiring. probably show base case on current burn and the q3 push as the point where we re-open offense. not gonna call it a reset. just bridge + targets.

also need to name the retention hole plainly -- logo retention is decent, usage on the core cohorts is better than the topline makes it look, but we still don't have the clean expansion/seat story in one place. Devon has pieces in Looker, CS has the renewal notes, none of it ties out clean enough for board yet. i'd rather say data gap than overclaim -- reason is they'll smell it immediately if we sand it down.

Yes — that’s the right spine. It is candid without turning the board update into an apology tour.

Suggested framing:

Slide: Bridge to the Q3 push

Headline:
“Bridge funding carries us through the current market and into the next operating milestone.”

Core message:
“We did not miss the product or team commitments we set for this period. The financing timeline changed as buyers paused and budgets became less predictable. This bridge gives us time to operate against the current plan and re-open offense around the Q3 push.”

Show explicitly:

- Bridge amount: $[X]
- Runway: [Y] months at current burn
- Funds:
  - Maintain current product and customer commitments
  - Complete the Q3 product/ GTM push
  - Reach [specific operating targets]
- No incremental hiring during the bridge
- No assumption of increased burn before the Q3 milestone
- Q3 decision point: re-open offense once [target 1], [target 2], and [target 3] are demonstrated

Avoid “reset.” The visual should be a timeline or bridge:

Current plan → bridge period → Q3 push → re-open offense

The important distinction is that the bridge buys time and evidence, not a new strategy.

Retention slide

Headline:
“Logo retention is healthy; expansion and usage are not yet reconciled cleanly enough.”

Suggested copy:

- Logo retention remains solid.
- Core-cohort usage is better than the topline view suggests.
- We do not yet have one reliable expansion/seat view tying together Looker, billing, and CS renewal notes.
- We are treating this as a data-quality and measurement gap—not claiming a stronger retention story than the underlying data supports.

A useful bottom panel:

What we know:
- Logo retention is decent.
- Mature cohorts show encouraging usage behavior.

What remains unresolved:
- Expansion ARR versus seat additions
- Usage decline versus annual-contract timing
- Looker data versus renewal-note definitions
- One reconciled cohort view for board reporting

Next step:
“Reconcile billing, product usage, and CS data into a single cohort-level view before making a stronger expansion claim.”

Spoken version:

“We’re not going to pretend the round slipped because we failed to execute. Against the product and team bar we set, we delivered. The timing changed because buyers froze and budgets got strange. The bridge is therefore not a reset; it is a way to fund the current plan through the Q3 push, with no hiring and a clear set of targets before we reopen offense.

On retention, the honest answer is that the logo picture is decent and the core cohorts look better than the topline suggests. But our expansion and seat story is not reconciled in one place yet. Devon has pieces in Looker, CS has renewal notes, and those do not tie out cleanly enough for us to overclaim. We’d rather call that a data gap now than have the board discover it for us.”

For the September and October 2023 external cohorts, 'entered the bounded Mercury flow' means an account entered the current bounded Mercury setup path used in the external package: invited into the product, able to access by the current invite / magic-link path, able to interact with preview-only sample data if present, and then progress toward connecting a real source and completing a first live sync. input.body:
March 2023 Board-Framing Case Study

Question
Did the financing miss reflect company execution, or did financing conditions change independently of delivery?

What we established
- Against the product and team commitments set for the period, the company delivered. The round did not slip because we missed those execution bars.
- The financing miss was primarily a timing and market-availability issue: buyers paused and budgets became less predictable.
- That distinction did not mean the operating story was complete. Logo retention was decent and core-cohort usage looked better than the topline, but expansion and seat data from Looker, billing, and CS notes did not reconcile cleanly enough for a stronger claim.

Board framing
Treat the financing outcome as a market/timing miss, not as proof of execution failure—and do not use that distinction to overstate the business. The bridge was a practical instrument to fund the existing plan through the Q3 push, with no incremental hiring and explicit operating targets before reopening offense.

Decision standard
Separate what was delivered, what the market delayed, and what evidence still needed reconciliation. The board story should be candid: execution held against the agreed bar; financing timing worsened; retention and expansion proof remained unfinished.

# 2024 Early-Call Debrief — Head of Customer Growth / GTM

Purpose

Use after each early candidate call to capture observed evidence and compare the slate against the same search criteria. The role is a hands-on customer-growth/GTM builder who can make Mercury- or Evergreen-like enterprise pull more repeatable. This is not a classic VP Sales mandate and is not permission to sell bespoke builds, one-off procurement work, custom permissions, or customer-specific roadmap branches.

Candidate:
Interviewer:
Date:
Call stage:
Relevant examples discussed:

Working standard

- Record concrete examples, actions, measures, and outcomes—not general impressions or overall hiring conclusions.
- Keep facts, interpretation, caveats, and follow-up questions separate.
- Use the same prompts and evidence standard for every candidate.
- Prefer attributable, dated evidence over logo count, pipeline size, enthusiasm, or polished frameworks.
- If an example is based mainly on founder-led demand, a single lighthouse account, or unusual support from an established team, note that limitation explicitly.

Assessment scale

- 1 — Little or no evidence; answer is mostly assertion, generic process, or future intent.
- 2 — Some relevant exposure, but evidence is narrow, dependent on special conditions, or weakly attributable.
- 3 — Credible evidence in a relevant setting, with meaningful caveats or limited proof of repeatability.
- 4 — Strong, specific evidence of the behavior across multiple examples or stages; remaining gaps are clear.
- 5 — Exceptional, directly attributable evidence that is repeatable and well measured in a comparable stage and context.

Do not average the scores mechanically. Explain the evidence, uncertainty, and what a later stage would need to test.

1. Repeatable enterprise adoption

Prompt

What evidence did the candidate provide that enterprise interest or adoption generalized beyond one account, logo, champion, or unusual circumstance?

Evidence

- Customer/account context:
- Candidate’s direct role:
- What changed in activation or onboarding:
- What changed in ongoing usage:
- Broader-team adoption or second use case:
- Retention or expansion outcome:
- What became reusable across accounts:
- Measures and dates:

Assessment: 1  2  3  4  5

Notes / caveats

- 

2. Judgment about not promising product

Prompt

How did the candidate handle a customer request that required an unshipped feature, bespoke build, roadmap commitment, or unusual exception?

Evidence

- Request and customer context:
- What the product could do at the time:
- What the candidate said or did:
- Resulting customer or account-team outcome:

Did the candidate distinguish clearly among

- Current product capability
- A workaround or bounded evaluation
- Product feedback
- A future possibility
- A commitment they were not authorized to make

Assessment: 1  2  3  4  5

Notes / caveats

- 

3. Ability to work without a mature sales organization

Prompt

What did the candidate personally build or operate when SDR, AE, CS, sales-ops, marketing, procurement, or other support infrastructure was limited or absent?

Evidence

- Manual work they owned directly:
- How they prioritized with limited capacity:
- Operating process or handoff they created:
- What they deliberately did not build yet:
- Evidence that the approach worked without founder-default escalation:
- Team or infrastructure assumptions:

Assessment: 1  2  3  4  5

Notes / caveats

- 

4. Technical-buyer comfort

Prompt

How has the candidate worked with technical buyers and cross-functional counterparts when the customer’s needs were technically specific, ambiguous, or not immediately shippable?

Evidence

- Buyer/persona and technical context:

input.body:
Date recorded: September 14, 2026
Historical event: February 13, 2023 lead-investor partner meeting

Purpose
Record the retention investigation Morgan wanted after the meeting, without smoothing the result into an investor narrative.

What prompted the investigation
- The lead-investor partner asked two pointed retention questions. One was hand-waved and the other was only half-answered.
- The visible top-line logo-retention view looked clean, but the usage cohort became unclear after roughly month 4, when teams moved into annual arrangements and seat expansion could hide underlying account decline.
- The problem was judged to be data integrity and interpretation—not slide labeling or deck polish.

Investigation requested
- Pull raw cohort cuts rather than rely on the blended view or a hand-shaped CSV.
- Show the month 3-to-month 6 shape clearly, then produce a real month-12 view, cohort by cohort.
- Report both logo retention and ARR/revenue retention.
- Separate expansions and seat additions from underlying retention so gross performance does not mask churn or make gross look like net.
- Include a sensitivity that removes the unusually large early customer / 2021 self-serve wave, so the result is not driven by a distorted denominator or one exceptional account.
- Reconcile the cuts against accounting and the warehouse, and check whether Stripe and application-event instrumentation are incomplete or misaligned.
- Explain, using the reconciled data, which part of the observed shape reflects genuine product improvement, which part is a segmentation artifact, and which part is an instrumentation problem.
- Produce one clean table before revising the retention slide or changing the broader plan.

Ownership and evidence standard
- Devon was asked to provide the real month-12 cut and lead the accounting/warehouse reconciliation.
- Anna Martinez and accounting were doing the cleanup and assembling the cuts; if a shaped draft was not available, the fallback was to work from the raw export.
- The result needed explicit cohort counts and definitions, with expansions/seat additions identified separately. It had to be plain enough to answer the partner’s question directly.

Immediate follow-up
- On February 14, Morgan reiterated the need for a cohort-by-cohort month-12 cut, with the 2021 self-serve wave and expansions that could hide churn stripped out, covering both logo and ARR.
- On February 15, Morgan again rejected the blended cut and asked for cohort-level month-12 retention with expansions/seat additions removed.
- The later March 2 board discussion confirmed that the blended story was insufficient and made the reconciled cohort-by-cohort month-12 analysis a Q2 deliverable, including the sensitivity excluding the unusually large early customer.

Interpretation
The requested work was not an effort to find a more favorable label or presentation. It was a reconstruction of the underlying retention evidence: follow accounts through time, distinguish net retention from expansion, test cohort definitions and instrumentation, and make the uncertainty visible before using retention in planning or investor materials.

[assistant · tmp] Webhook signature verification

Atlas signs each webhook with the workspace’s webhook secret. Verify the signature before parsing or acting on the event.

1. Read the required headers

Read these headers from the incoming request:

- `X-Scaffold-Workspace`
- `X-Scaffold-Signature`

HTTP header names are case-insensitive, so `x-scaffold-signature` is also accepted by the supported path. Underscore-style names, such as `x_scaffold_signature`, and query-parameter fallbacks are not supported.

The signature header has this form:

```text
t=<unix_timestamp>,v1=<hex_signature>
```

2. Preserve the raw request body

Capture the request body as received, before JSON parsing, whitespace normalization, field reordering, or reserialization. The signature is calculated over the raw body, not over a newly serialized JSON object.

3. Recreate the signature base string

Use the timestamp from the `t` value and the raw request body to construct the base string:

```text
<timestamp>.<raw_request_body>
```

Compute the HMAC-SHA256 digest of that base string with the webhook secret, then compare the resulting hexadecimal value with the `v1` value. Use a constant-time comparison.

Subject: Holiday coverage / week of Dec 18–22

Hi team,

A few reminders for the week before Christmas so people can plan cleanly:

1. Support and on-call coverage
- The named support coverage and engineering on-call assignments already listed in the support rotation doc stay active.
- If you are a named owner in the support rotation doc, please keep an eye on your normal queue and handoff notes.
- Everyone else can assume reduced response expectations unless directly tagged by the named owner.

2. Standing meetings
- Managers and meeting owners should review recurring meetings for Dec 18–22 and cancel any session that is not truly needed.
- If a standing meeting does happen, please keep it short and decision-specific.

3. Async updates
- Even if meetings are canceled, please continue posting normal async updates in your usual project/channel cadence so people out later in the month can reconstruct status.
- Function leads should post an end-of-day summary in their team channel on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and owners should drop in quick notes when a task moves, slips, or changes shape.

4. Escalations
- If anything feels urgent, potentially customer-impacting, or cross-functional, raise it in the main channel for your area and tag the relevant leads so someone can pick it up quickly.
- For support issues, start with the named support owner from the support rotation doc, but if you are unsure, err on the side of tagging broadly.
- If a question sits for more than an hour, please repost it with extra context so the right group sees it.

Thanks,
HR

15-minute Thanksgiving-week leadership check-in

- 0:00–2:00 — Frame and triage
  - Goal: identify only customer-impacting, time-bound, or genuinely cross-functional items.
  - No founder-only blocker is assumed. Routine cleanup stays with the named owner; Devon is not the default escalation path.

- 2:00–9:00 — Owner round: one prompt each
  - Sarah — Which customer/account threads need action before Monday, and what is the exact next step and owner? Keep routine follow-up in the account lane.
  - Jake — Any Mercury activation, sync, or production issue requiring action this week? Anything can wait until normal sequencing resumes?
  - Leo — Any Atlas/platform reliability, data-integrity, auth, or release issue with customer impact? Otherwise route through support/Jake.
  - Priya — Any activation/onboarding issue causing active customer blockage or a committed-date risk? Defer copy or experiment discussion unless time-sensitive.
  - Anna — Any renewal-risk or evidence item with a dated source and a decision needed now? Do not turn thin evidence into an exec issue.
  - Devon — Only: is there a commercial/procurement exception, renewal decision, or true cofounder judgment call? No routine account cleanup.
  - Morgan — What, if anything, requires a founder decision today? Confirm the customer/board narrative remains factual and bounded.

- 9:00–12:00 — Apply escalation thresholds
  - Escalate live only for: customer-impacting outage/data issue/security or legal concern; an external commitment or contract deadline before Monday; nonstandard pricing, scope, or customer promise; or a cross-functional blocker with no in-lane resolution and a named near-term deadline.
  - A founder escalation must include the decision requested, accountable owner, deadline, consequence of waiting, and why the named owner cannot resolve it.
  - “Important,” “visible,” or “needs cleanup” alone is not an escalation threshold.

- 12:00–14:00 — Explicit deferrals
  - Defer routine account-thread cleanup, broad customer reviews, nonurgent follow-ups, internal evidence grooming, and ordinary Mercury/Atlas sequencing until after the holiday week.
  - Defer granular-admin/role-scope discussion, roadmap implications, expansion framing, and any broader customer or GTM narrative. Keep Evergreen usage/commercial treatment factual and separate from advanced-admin scope.

- 14:00–15:00 — Close with a bounded coverage list
  - Record only: item, named owner, next action, deadline, and escalation status.
  - Everything else is explicitly marked “defer until after holiday week”; no loose-owner queue for Devon, and no new standing meetings or broad async updates during quiet coverage.

input.body:
Historical handoff note
Date: 2026-09-14
Scope: Mercury activation/onboarding surface work, recorded from the June–July 2023 handoff decisions.

Purpose
Keep design decisions, implementation risk, and release gating in separate, auditable lanes. The handoff does not expand Mercury scope or imply that unresolved risk was solved.

Ownership
- Priya — design owner. Owns activation/onboarding UX calls, flow decisions, copy, states, and the Figma source of truth. The reviewed Figma v0.2 branches and locked CTA labels were canonical for that pass; new state exploration was not part of the handoff.
- Marcus — implementation and release-readiness owner. Owns translation of the approved design into implementation gates, QA readiness, dogfood blockers, and release review. The Linear implementation checklist and release review are canonical for these concerns.
- Leo — technical/platform-seam read when a risk crosses into auth, source-state, or platform behavior; not the owner of ordinary design calls.
- Jake — weekly sequencing and ledger coordination; keeps the work moving from the launch-readiness ledger but does not replace Priya’s design ownership or Marcus’s release gate.
- Anna — verifies activation-event definitions and mapping where the release gate depends on instrumentation.

Where decisions belonged
- Product/design decisions: Priya in Figma. This includes the reviewed activation branches, CTA labels, copy, state descriptions, and whether a proposed UX change is in the agreed design.
- Implementation and release-readiness decisions: Marcus in the Linear checklist and release review. This includes server role plus source-state rendering, invite edge cases, honest queued-sync status, normalized failure buckets, idempotent retry, exclusion of sample paths from activation eventing, and dogfood gates.
- Technical/platform interpretation: Leo when the question is an auth, source-state, or platform-seam behavior question.
- Coordination and sequencing: Jake through the single Mercury launch-readiness ledger. Risks should not be left scattered across pull requests, Figma comments, or Discord.

How disagreements should be resolved
1. Classify the disagreement before debating it: design choice, implementation/release risk, instrumentation definition, or platform-seam behavior.
2. Route it to the owning canonical artifact: Figma for design; the Linear checklist/release review for readiness; the event-definition record for instrumentation; Leo for a technical/platform interpretation.
3. Keep the existing decision stable unless new evidence requires a change. A release-risk concern is not automatically a design veto, and a Figma-ready state is not automatically safe to ship.
4. Record the concrete issue, evidence, owner, acceptance condition, and disposition in the launch-readiness ledger. Discord and comment threads should link back to that record rather than become competing sources of truth.
5. If the issue crosses lanes or remains material, Priya and Marcus review it together, with Leo or Anna pulled in only for the relevant technical or eventing question. Jake coordinates the next checkpoint; Morgan resolves only a genuinely cross-functional scope or priority decision, not routine owner-lane disputes.
6. Do not silently broaden the flow. The June 2023 handoff treated sample-data activation, invited-member rendering, queued-sync honesty, and failed-sync clarity/retry as explicit release gates; setup-guide copy, narrow-width preview-card spacing, and failed-state icon polish were follow-up polish rather than launch blockers.

Historical decision
The team explicitly separated Priya’s design calls in Figma from Marcus’s release-readiness and dogfood gating in the implementation checklist and release review. The routing was clarified because the underlying Priya/Marcus tension was not resolved by simply posting in Discord. The durable rule is to preserve the design decision in its owner lane, surface implementation risk in the release ledger, and resolve disagreements using evidence and explicit acceptance criteria.

2. Route it to the owning canonical artifact: Figma for design; the Linear checklist/release review for readiness; the event-definition record for instrumentation; Leo for a technical/platform interpretation.
3. Keep the existing decision stable unless new evidence requires a change. A release-risk concern is not automatically a design veto, and a Figma-ready state is not automatically safe to ship.
4. Record the concrete issue, evidence, owner, acceptance condition, and disposition in the launch-readiness ledger. Discord and comment threads should link back to that record rather than become competing sources of truth.
5. If the issue crosses lanes or remains material, Priya and Marcus review it together, with Leo or Anna pulled in only for the relevant technical or eventing question. Jake coordinates the next checkpoint; Morgan resolves only a genuinely cross-functional scope or priority decision, not routine owner-lane disputes.
6. Do not silently broaden the flow. The June 2023 handoff treated sample-data activation, invited-member rendering, queued-sync honesty, and failed-sync clarity/retry as explicit release gates; setup-guide copy, narrow-width preview-card spacing, and failed-state icon polish were follow-up polish rather than launch blockers.

Historical decision
The team explicitly separated Priya’s design calls in Figma from Marcus’s release-readiness and dogfood gating in the implementation checklist and release review. The routing was clarified because the underlying Priya/Marcus tension was not resolved by simply posting in Discord. The durable rule is to preserve the design decision in its owner lane, surface implementation risk in the release ledger, and resolve disagreements using evidence and explicit acceptance criteria.

arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist

Date: January 21, 2025
Purpose: Make a narrow set of internal signals produce a named next action and better account follow-up. This is an owner checklist, not a scorecard.

## Operating boundary
- [ ] Keep v0.1 with the current owners: Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, and Sarah Kim. No new hiring lane or requisition.
- [ ] Keep January Mercury activation—workspace, first source, first live sync, and teammate-invite/admin-role basics—as the center of gravity. Compass gets only enough seam work to test these actions.
- [ ] Do not build a board dashboard, prettier internal dashboard, generic health score, investor package, or new product surface.
- [ ] Every signal must change a named account-team action; otherwise it stays an internal FYI or is dropped.

## 1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction follow-up
- [ ] Signal: A named account shows a specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion plausibly contributing to apparent renewal risk. Do not combine product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one category.
- [ ] Trigger/action: Route to the named account owner for a defined follow-up on the specific friction; Nadia turns it into an account-team script only after the evidence bar is met. No generic “renewal risk” outreach.
- [ ] Who sees it: First Sarah and Nadia; then the named account owner. Keep it internal until the evidence and caveat bundle is complete. Do not broadly circulate as a health label.
- [ ] Evidence/caveat: Include the account, concrete friction, date/context, and what is observed versus inferred. Anna attaches the definition and caveat: this is an apparent-risk explanation, not proof of churn, product weakness, or causal retention impact.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: Sarah classifies the underlying thread note as reliable, mixed, or too thin and separates customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation. Mixed notes carry an explicit caveat; too-thin notes remain internal and cannot drive outreach.
- [ ] Owners: Anna—definition/caveat; Sarah—source hygiene and customer-thread continuity; Nadia—pattern capture and follow-up script; Jake—sequencing if product behavior is implicated; Leo—data/platform seam check where the event path needs verification.
- [ ] Not building: No renewal-risk score, churn model, board-facing risk view, or product/permissions fix inferred from a single account note.

## 2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- [ ] Signal: A workspace has completed a real first live sync and the teammate-invite/admin-role basics are visible enough to ground a next action.
- [ ] Trigger/action: Prompt the account team to ask the smallest useful next-use question or take a specific customer-growth follow-up action. Do not send generic upsell language.
- [ ] Who sees it: First Nadia and the relevant account owner, with Sarah maintaining the live thread. Jake sees sequencing implications; Leo sees the data/platform seam before anything leaves the current team.
- [ ] Evidence/caveat: Show the actual first-live-sync event and the visible invite/admin-role state. Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage; first sync is not proof of expansion intent, repeatability, or retention.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: Use a traceable event path plus a source-tagged account note where customer context is included. Leo must confirm the seam is defendable; Sarah must identify whether the note is reliable, mixed, or too thin. Inference alone cannot trigger customer outreach.
- [ ] Owners: Jake—keep the trigger late enough and aligned with Mercury activation; Leo—data/platform seam check; Nadia—prompt and follow-up logic; Sarah—account context/thread; Anna—definition and caveat.
- [ ] Not building: No expansion dashboard, automated upsell engine, readiness score, new product surface, or bespoke Evergreen/customer branch.

## 3. Account-note source quality gate
- [ ] Signal: An account note is proposed for use in a Compass follow-up and has an explicit provenance and quality state.
- [ ] Trigger/action: Sarah labels the note reliable, mixed, or too thin; Nadia routes only the reliable or explicitly caveated mixed inputs into a named follow-up. Too-thin notes stay internal and trigger source cleanup, not outreach.
- [ ] Who sees it: Sarah first; Nadia and the relevant owner next. Anna sees caveat/definition issues; Jake and Leo see only items requiring sequencing or seam review. Do not expose unqualified notes as clean signals.
- [ ] Evidence/caveat: Preserve source, date/context, and provenance: customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation. Anna ensures the caveat travels with the signal; Nadia does not treat internal inference as customer fact.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: A real follow-up requires a traceable source and enough detail to identify the account, event/friction, and next action. Record uncertainty and missing fields explicitly; do not backfill confidence from repetition of an unverified note.
- [ ] Owners: Sarah—quality classification, provenance, and account continuity; Nadia—routing and pattern capture; Anna—definitions/caveats; Jake—execution/sequencing; Leo—technical evidence path when applicable.
- [ ] Not building: No universal note-scoring system, cleanup-only reporting layer, automatic customer outreach, or dashboard that hides weak provenance.

## v0.1 completion check
- [ ] For each signal, the team can name the action, first viewer, evidence/caveat bundle, source-quality bar, and explicit non-goal.
- [ ] Test whether the signal changes account behavior or follow-up. If it only produces a label or prettier reporting, narrow it or stop.
- [ ] Revisit the operating model only if v0.1 demonstrates real behavior change or repeatable account follow-up—not because Compass has a name.
